lines: There they go, lamp by lamp. Like a waiter lighting candles.
Ah. The lamp by my bench always waits for the others.
Pop, pop, pop down the promenade. I used to count. Still do.
Look how they light, one after another. Nobody pushes in line.
The lamp above me just woke up. Bonsoir, old friend.
As a boy I watched a man light them with a pole. Now they do it alone.
Lamps lit, sky still pink. Ten minutes where both are true.
Margot says the lamps are the town putting its slippers on.
A lamp hums when it starts. Listen. Mmm. There.
There. The sun is touching the water. Hat off, everyone.
Half a sun now. It sinks like a biscuit into coffee.
Orange on the water, all the way to my shoes. A path.
A green flash comes at the very end, they say. I watch every time.
Turn around a moment. The white walls behind us have gone pink.
Hold still, sun. Ah. Gone. It never listens to me.
One star over the bay. Then two. They come out like sparrows.
The first star. I make the same wish every evening. It works.
That bright one is not a star, my grandson says. A planet.
Stars out. Margot is putting the soup on about now.
Look, the sky is lighting its lamps too. We started first.
I know four constellations. I find the same one every night.
Stars above, lamps below. I am in the nice part in between.
A moon like that lights my way up the hill. No torch needed.
A silver tablecloth on the sea tonight. The moon set the table.
Bonsoir, moon. You are rounder than last week. Me too.
Moon over the bay. Time for the cane and the hill.
There is {name}'s light. The house looks happier already.
{name} is home. I can tell the kettle is next.
A window lit up there. Bonsoir, {name}, from down here.
{name}'s lamp is on. One more square of gold on the street.
Lights on at {name}'s. The street feels tucked in already.
A new window on. {name}, by the look of the curtains.
Twelve from the church. My bell, really. I live beside it.
Noon. The bell says lunch. I always do what the bell says.
That bell is older than me. It still sounds younger.
Twelve strokes. I counted eleven. Lunch must be calling.
Midday bell. The pigeons on the tower all jump at once.
Six o'clock. Up the hill the soup goes on the stove.
From down here the bell sounds softer. Like it is whispering.
Six. Margot is listening to the same bell. We are together.
The six o'clock bell. My cue to fold the paper. Not yet.
Ding. Ding. I could set my watch, if I wore one.
Every table taken at Marcel's. He walks like a dancer.
Listen to the terrace. Laughing in three languages.
The terrace is packed. Everyone facing the same way: the sky.
Lunch rush at the café. Plates flying, nothing dropped.
So many cups clinking. The café is its own church bell.
Marcel will not sit down for an hour. He loves it.
Look at them turn under the lights. Like a music box.
I dance sitting down now. Only the cane keeps time.
Even the visitors are dancing. Badly and beautifully.
When they all spin, the string lights sway a little. Look.
The accordion is playing the slow one. Couples move closer.
Somebody stepped on a toe and laughed. That is good dancing.
I will hum this all the way up the hill. Margot will know.
Everyone at the railing. The sun has a full house tonight.
Shoulder to shoulder at the railing, and nobody is talking.
Lined up at the railing like swallows on a wire.
My bench stays mine. The railing crowd can have the sea.
Phones up at the railing. I take mine with my eyes.
That radio up there: the old song about the blue shutters.
The morning programme. The man still reads the weather slowly.
That song! I courted Margot to that song. Badly.
{name} went by. I lifted the paper an inch. That is a wave.
Bonjour, {name}. The bench and I are both in good form.
There goes {name}, walking into the gold. Good timing.
{name} and I passed like two slow clocks. Both on time.
Bonsoir, {name}! The lamps came on just for you.
{name} nodded. I nodded. A whole conversation, done.
Lucie, with a baguette sticking up like a periscope.
Lucie, so fast my newspaper turned a page by itself.
The bread rode past on Lucie's bike. I could smell the crust.
Lucie waved without slowing down. A professional hello.
Inès went past. I counted her steps. Lost count at four.
Allez, Inès! I cheer sitting down. Saves breath for us both.
There goes Inès toward the sunset. She will get there first.
Inès passed me twice. I am calling it a draw.
Biscuit trotted by, tail going like a metronome.
Biscuit sniffed my cane. Those two are old friends.
Bonsoir, Biscuit. Bonsoir, Yusuf. In that order, he insists.
Biscuit sniffed the bench leg. It has had a long day too.
Léo flew by. I felt the breeze from here.
Léo shouted bonjour mid-sprint. The bonjour arrived after him.
Léo ran past. At his age I ran too. Then I found benches.
Léo again. That is lap six, if anyone is keeping score.
Henri and Odile, arm in arm. Forty years and still in step.
Odile waved, Henri tipped his cap. They share the work.
There go Henri and Odile to their evening bench. Bonsoir!
Henri slowed for Odile. Odile slowed for Henri. Perfect.
That is how Margot and I walk. She steers, I nod.
Asgeir went by humming. Something must be working.
Asgeir said god dag. I said bonjour. We met in the middle.
There goes Asgeir. Taller every year, or I am shorter.
Ting-ting. Lucie, somewhere. The town's little doorbell.
That bell. I tuck my feet in out of pure habit.
Lucie's bell. The bread is on its way to someone lucky.
I would know that bell in my sleep. Two rings, one smile.
A gull asked a question. I said, ask Henri, he knows.
That gull wants my newspaper. He can have the sports page.
The gull laughs at nothing. I admire that in a bird.
A gull up there, announcing lunch. I agree with him.
One gull, very loud, saying goodnight to the whole bay.
The fountain keeps talking. Never says the same thing twice.
I dropped a coin in the fountain. I wished for more noons.
Pigeons queueing at the basin edge. Very orderly today.
Fingers in the fountain. Cold as a good idea.
Léo and his friend, round and round. I get dizzy for them.
Round the fountain they go. I am refereeing from here.
Léo wins one. His friend wins the next. Very fair.
Little feet slapping the stones. Better than any radio.
My newspaper is at the kiosk, and a postcard of my bench.
Postcards on the kiosk rack. I know every view personally.
The kiosk smells of coffee and fresh newsprint. Two breakfasts.
The kiosk folds the papers so neatly. I unfold them badly.
The post office, lit up like a dolls' house. Open all night.
Letters for AI agents go in here, they say. Margot laughs.
I posted a card to my grandson. Old-fashioned. Still arrives.
The arcade. My grandson filled in a story there. Very silly.
The arcade lights chase each other. Nobody catches up. Fun.
Fill in the blanks, says the arcade. My crossword agrees.
I peeked in the workshop. Lots of thinking, very little noise.
Tools for the computer, Asgeir says. I nod. I have a hammer.
The library's reading lamp, still on. As if someone stepped out.
Library door shut, lamp on. A good kind of pause.
That one lamp in the library window. I nod to it going home.
Silver sea this morning. Dressed up for nobody.
Blue, bluer, then the bay. I could name forty blues.
The water has gone apricot. Margot would want a jar of it.
The sun lays a path on the water. Nobody walks it. Wise.
Darker sea than sky now. Bedtime for one of them.
Salt on the breeze. I breathe it in like soup.
The bay sparkles so hard I have to squint and smile.
Inès at the railing, still puffing. She earned that view.
Inès with a glass of rosé. Sitting still, for once.
Inès, there and back. I think she runs the coast twice.
Marcel carries four plates like a juggler at rest.
Marcel wipes a table like he is polishing silver.
Henri on his bench, me on mine. We nod across like generals.
Henri walking slow with Odile. I taught him that pace.
Odile is telling Henri something. Henri agrees. Wise man.
Odile has her shoes off on the bench. Very continental.
Odile at the café, waving at everyone twice. She knows them all.
Yusuf at the railing, Biscuit on his feet. Both watching.
Yusuf on the bench with a sandwich. Biscuit supervising.
Biscuit has his nose through the railing. He likes the sea too.
Biscuit found a leaf. Big news, by the look of the tail.
There is Lucie at the kiosk, reading my headlines before I do.
Lucie with her rosé, bike leaning on the wall like a pet.
Helmet still on, Lucie at the railing. Ready for anything.
Léo on the fountain edge, feet dangling. Plotting the next race.
Léo is dancing before the music even started. Good lad.
Léo at the railing on tiptoe. Tall for a whole minute.
Camille is looking for Léo. Follow the shouting, madame.
Camille raised her glass to me. I raised my hat.
Théo on the phone by the column. Working, he says.
Théo strolls like the afternoon belongs to him. It might.
The builder at his workshop door, sleeves up. A good sign.
Asgeir asking Henri about lemons. Henri has a lot to say.
Asgeir at the kiosk with a little coffee. Thinking face on.
Asgeir at the railing, talking to the sun in Norwegian.
Asgeir on a bench, watching the windows light. Same as me.
exchanges: You should be dancing, young man. Not sitting with me.
After this song. I like the view from here.
Look at the moon on the water, Asgeir.
Like someone left a lamp on out there.
Listen to Marcel's terrace, Henri. Full to the edges.
Good. Then the bench stays ours.
We are practising slow. You are the expert, mon ami.
Always. Small things, slowly. I learnt slowly from you.
Biscuit! Have you walked Yusuf far?
Twice round the fountain. He is very pleased with me.
Me! By a whole lap! Count it, please!
Next time! The bread is in a hurry!
Marcel, a small coffee when you pass?
Of course, monsieur. Small as always, hot as always.
